records.title: Arazzo Extensions
records.subtitle: The Arazzo vendor extensions <rapi-flow> supports - x-security, x-operation and x-allowReserved as Redocly Respect defines them, and its own x-mock-server-status-code.
records.content: <rapi-flow> supports three vendor extensions of Arazzo, as Redocly Respect defines them. They work in runs, in the diagram and in the MCP export. A fourth, x-mock-server-status-code, is RapiDoc's own and only fills the run panel's mock table. | Extension | On | What it does | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | x-security | workflow, step | The credentials a request sends. | | x-operation | step | Calls a URL outside the API sources. | | x-allowReserved | step parameter | Sends reserved characters in a query value unencoded. | | x-mock-server-status-code | step | The status codes the mock answers this st

records.title: Credentials in the workflow (x-security)
records.subtitle: Arazzo Extensions
records.content: <rapi-flow> supports the x-security extension of Redocly Respect, so an Arazzo spec can say which credentials each request sends instead of relying on what the reader typed into the Authentication section. Put it on a step, or on the workflow for every step: - Each entry has either schemeName (a scheme in the step's source's components.securitySchemes) or an inline scheme, plus values: apiKey for an API key (in: header, query or cookie), username and password for HTTP Basic, token for HTTP Beare

records.title: Calls outside the API sources (x-operation)
records.subtitle: Arazzo Extensions
records.content: A step can call an endpoint that no source description describes, such as a file download link an earlier step returned, or a third-party API, with the x-operation extension of Redocly Respect. It takes the place of operationId: - url is an absolute http or https URL, or a runtime expression; {$inputs.x} can be interpolated into a URL too. method is any HTTP method, in any case. - parameters work as for other steps: query, header and cookie values are added, and a path parameter fills its {name}

records.title: Reserved characters in query values (x-allowReserved)
records.subtitle: Arazzo Extensions
records.content: Query values are percent-encoded, so https://a.example/x is sent as https%3A%2F%2Fa.example%2Fx. When the API expects the value as is (a URL, a filter expression), set x-allowReserved: true on the step's parameter, the Arazzo counterpart of OpenAPI's allowReserved, as in Redocly Respect: The reserved characters : / ? [ ] @ ! $ & ' ( ) + , ; = are then sent unencoded; spaces and other characters are still encoded, and so is , which would end the URL's query. A query parameter with allowReserved:

records.title: Mock status codes (x-mock-server-status-code)
records.subtitle: Arazzo Extensions
records.content: A workflow that shows a failure path, a retry or a goto, can carry the scenario it needs. Put the codes on the step, in the syntax of the mock-server-status-code attribute: The value fills the step's row of the run panel's Mock Response Status table, where the reader can change it before a run: codes without a prefix are used in turn, one per attempt; random: picks one at random. records.title: RapiFlow
records.subtitle: Draw the workflows of an Arazzo spec as a diagram next to your API reference with <rapi-flow>, and run them in the browser against the API or a mock.
records.content: An API reference shows operations one at a time. Integrators also need the order: find a pet, check it, order it, read the order back. Arazzo describes those sequences, and <rapi-flow> draws them: one box per step, linked to its operation, the values each step passes on, and the success and failure branches. Readers can run a workflow from the page and watch each step answer. The RapiFlow page runs a workflow against the in-browser mock, the rapi-flow example puts the diagram next to a full API reference, and the multi-API example pairs it with one <rapi-doc-mini> per API. Load it <rapi-flow>

records.title: Load it
records.subtitle: RapiFlow
records.content: <rapi-flow> is a separate bundle, rapidoc-flow-min.js (import 'rapidoc/flow' with a bundler), so pages that only use <rapi-doc> don't download it. It carries its own copy of Lit and the Arazzo runtime; rapidoc-min.js carries no Arazzo code. The Quickstart puts both on a page and runs a workflow against the in-browser mock.

records.title: Standalone or paired
records.subtitle: RapiFlow
records.content: - Paired (for="<id>"): the element uses that <rapi-doc>'s OpenAPI spec, its selected server and the credentials entered in its Authentication section. Clicking a step scrolls the reference to the step's operation. If the <rapi-doc> has mock-server="true", runs go to the in-browser mock. records.title: In a developer portal
records.subtitle: RapiFlow
records.content: @rapidoc/portal draws workflows in docs pages with the Markdoc tag: the diagram is rendered as static SVG at build time, and rapidoc-flow-min.js loads only when a reader clicks Run workflow . The portal build also turns each workflow into an MCP tool for rapidoc serve's /mcp endpoint.

records.subtitle: Running Workflows
records.content: A workflow is easiest to show and test before the API exists, or without touching real data.

records.title: The in-browser mock
records.subtitle: Running Workflows
records.content: Turn on mock-server on the paired elements. Every request of the run to their APIs is answered in the page from the OpenAPI spec's examples and schemas; the Execution Log's heading reads "Execution Log (mocked responses)" when every response was mocked; when only some were (a source with no mocking element), those entries say "mocked response" when opened. records.title: Slots & Styling
records.subtitle: Put your own markup in <rapi-flow>, style it with CSS parts, and read its properties.
records.content: Every attribute, method and event of <rapi-flow> is on its API reference page, read from the element's source. All its events bubble and cross the shadow boundary (composed). Slots Put your own markup at the top or bottom of the element with slot="header" or slot="footer": a logo, a title, a server switch, links. It stays in the page's DOM, so the page's CSS styles it and its scripts find it, and it scrolls with the diagram. Its spacing is yours: the element adds none around it. | Slot | Where | | :--- | :--- | | header | At the top, above the card with the Arazzo spec's URL and API sources. |

records.title: Styling
records.subtitle: Slots & Styling
records.content: theme and color-scheme work as on <rapi-doc>, and the element reads the same CSS custom properties. Its CSS parts: mcp-export, document (the card with the URL and the API sources), sources, url, url-form, url-input, url-load, url-error, header, title, select, description, view-toggle, diagram, run, run-inputs, run-button, run-stop, log-toggle (the Execution Log's Single line / Multiline switch), message, problems.

records.title: Properties
records.subtitle: Slots & Styling
records.content: The element also exposes arazzoDocument (the parsed document), workflowRuntimeSource, which a paired <rapi-doc> uses to add workflow tools to its MCP export, and the statusCodes property that fills the Mock Response Status table (see Running against a mock).
